displayQuote: The Male Libido is Like Being Chained to a Madman

meta.title: Who really said "The Male Libido is Like Being Chained to a Madman"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to David Niven, Socrates and Kingsley Amis. The thought is Sophocles’, in Plato’s Republic — but the famous wording is in no translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Male Libido is Like Being Chained to a Madman'?
meta.ogDescription: Sophocles said something like it, through Cephalus, in Plato’s Republic. Niven said a version on screen. Nobody wrote it this way.

answer.label: Not David Niven — a modern paraphrase of Sophocles
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely ancient. In Book 1 of Plato’s “Republic,” the old man Cephalus recalls asking Sophocles whether age had cost him his appetite for love, and reports the poet’s relief at escaping it. But no published translation reads “the male libido is like being chained to a madman” — that compression is modern, and David Niven’s connection to it is a line of film dialogue, not authorship.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Sophocles, as relayed by Cephalus to Socrates
Benjamin Jowett — public domain, read in full at Project Gutenberg
A 1941 translation by Francis Macdonald Cornford: “it is like escaping from bondage to a raging madman”
He spoke a paraphrase as Peter Carter in “A Matter of Life and Death” (1946)

source.excerpt: How well I remember the aged poet Sophocles, when in answer to the question, How does love suit with age, Sophocles,—are you still the man you were? Peace, he replied; most gladly have I escaped the thing of which you speak; I feel as if I had escaped from a mad and furious master.
trail: Quote Investigator’s study of the saying ↗ traces the whole family of “libido” similes back to Book 1 of Plato’s “Republic,” and explains the tangle of credits as a transmission problem: the remark passes from Sophocles to Cephalus to Socrates and then to Plato’s page, so each of them has been named as its author.

We read the passage ourselves in Jowett’s public-domain translation at Project Gutenberg ↗ rather than relying on a summary. It reads “I feel as if I had escaped from a mad and furious master” — which is not the famous wording.

QI transcribes four translations and no two agree: “a frantic and savage master” (1852), “a mad and furious master” (Jowett), “bondage to a raging madman” (1941, Francis Macdonald Cornford — a surname QI’s own citation spells “Cornfield”) and “a sort of frenzied and savage master” (Bloom). Only the 1941 version supplies both the bondage and the madman, which is why the modern aphorism resembles it most.

On the David Niven link, QI quotes the exchange ↗ from “A Matter of Life and Death” (1946) ↗, written and directed by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger: Niven’s character attributes the line to Sophocles on screen. QI’s only citation for that dialogue is a YouTube upload, which we did not treat as a transcript, so we report the exchange as QI’s transcription rather than as verified film text.
source.excerptNote: Benjamin Jowett’s translation of “The Republic,” Book 1, read directly from the Project Gutenberg text. Cephalus is the speaker; the words after “Peace, he replied” are Sophocles’. Note what is not here: no chain, and no madman — Jowett has “a mad and furious master.”

source.rightsNote: Plato’s Greek has been out of copyright for centuries, and the Jowett translation quoted above is public domain — you can read the whole of it free at Project Gutenberg. The famous wording is a different matter: it matches no published translation we could find, so it has no identifiable author, publisher or date, and we assert no rights status for it. The 1941 translation it most resembles remains in copyright.

author.name: Sophocles
author.heading: About Sophocles
author.bio: Sophocles was one of the three Athenian tragedians whose work survives, and by some distance the most successful of them in his own lifetime: he entered thirty dramatic competitions, won twenty-four, and was never placed lower than second. Of more than 120 plays, seven survive complete, among them Antigone and Oedipus Rex. He lived into his nineties, which is why Plato could plausibly cast him as the authority on what old age does to desire.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Quote Investigator lists eight candidates for this one line. The reason is structural rather than careless: in Plato’s text the remark is quoted inside a quotation inside a dialogue, so four different people can each look like the speaker.

items.why: Russell Brand’s 2007 memoir “My Booky Wook” has “Socrates says the male libido is like being chained to a madman,” and QI records that this is the earliest “chained” instance it found ↗. Socrates is the listener in the scene, not the speaker.
Plato wrote the dialogue down, which makes him the author of the book but not of the remark. QI attributes the analogy to Sophocles “in The Republic” ↗, and the work itself ↗ is his.

items.tag: Recited it, did not write it
items.why: Niven delivered a version as Peter Carter in “A Matter of Life and Death” (1946) — and in the scene his character explicitly credits Sophocles. The screenplay was by Powell and Pressburger; an actor speaking a scripted paraphrase is not its author.

A 2001 “Guardian” profile quotes Paul Whitehouse recalling Amis saying his libido’s retirement was like being released after “50 years… chained to an idiot,” as QI documents ↗. That is a second-hand recollection of a variant, from 2001.

items.who: Any of them, as usually quoted
items.why: The sentence in circulation is a modern compression. QI’s own conclusion ↗ is that the translations “founded an evolving family of sayings,” moving from “escaped,” “savage” and “master” toward “chained” and “madman” over time.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s finding ↗: the analogy belongs to Sophocles as reported in “The Republic,” the multiple credits come from the nested framing of the quotation, and the familiar “chained to a madman” phrasing is a late arrival in an evolving family of sayings.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cephalus is not complaining about old age — he is defending it. The whole point of the passage is that the losses people dread turn out to feel like release, and Sophocles is his star witness: desire was not a pleasure but a tyrant, and age fired it.

That argument opens the “Republic,” and it sets up everything after it. Before Plato can ask what justice is, he needs a speaker calm enough to ask the question — so the dialogue begins by clearing the passions out of the room.
detailsBody: The reason this quote has eight claimants is worth spelling out, because it is a useful lesson in how attributions decay. Plato writes a dialogue in which Socrates reports a conversation with Cephalus, in which Cephalus reports a conversation with Sophocles. Strip one layer and Cephalus becomes the speaker; strip two and it is Socrates; strip three and it is Plato.

Translation then does the rest. Each English version reaches for different words — a savage master, a furious master, a raging madman — and the aphorism that finally stuck in the 21st century belongs to none of them. It is the shape of the thought that survived, not the sentence.
context.pull: Desire was not a pleasure but a tyrant, and age fired it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the “libido” simile to Book 1 of Plato’s Republic, where Cephalus relays a remark of Sophocles, and attributes the multiple credits to that nested framing.

Quote Investigator transcribes the 1941 Cornford translation as “it is like escaping from bondage to a raging madman” and records Russell Brand’s 2007 memoir crediting Socrates with “chained to a madman.”
Jowett’s public-domain translation of Republic Book 1 reads “I feel as if I had escaped from a mad and furious master” — read directly in the Project Gutenberg text.
Sophocles lived c. 497/496 to winter 406/405 BC, wrote more than 120 plays with seven surviving complete, and won 24 of 30 competitions.
A Matter of Life and Death (1946) is a film by Emeric Pressburger and Michael Powell starring David Niven.
